name: Asarela
title: Levitical singer and musician under David
summary: Asarela (also called Jesarela) was a son of the music leader Asaf and belonged to the tribe of Levi. He was one of the singers and musicians in the organized worship service that King David established. The musical service is described in Chronicles as a form of prophetic activity, where the singers prophesied with harps, lyres, and cymbals under the king's supervision. David organized 24 divisions of singers in preparation for the temple that Solomon would later build. By lot, Jesarela – who is identical to Asarela – was assigned the seventh division, together with twelve relatives. This prophetic musical service emphasizes that singing and worship in Israelite religion were not merely aesthetic expression but were understood as spiritually inspired proclamation before God's face.

keyEvents.title: Appointment to Prophetic Musical Service
keyEvents.description: Asarela was appointed as one of Asaph's sons to prophesy with harps, lyres, and cymbals in the worship service. He served under the direct leadership of his father Asaph, who in turn was under the king's supervision.

keyEvents.title: Lot Casting for the Seventh Service Shift
keyEvents.description: By lot, Jesarela (identified with Asarela) was assigned to the seventh shift in the musical service. He and his twelve relatives made up this shift among the 24 divisions of singers that David organized as preparation for temple service.

versions.summary: Asarelah was a son of Asaph, the famous worship leader during King David's time. He served as one of the Levitical singers and musicians in temple service, appointed by lot to lead worship. His service was part of the organized praise that David established for God's house.
versions.title: Levitical singer in the temple
versions.reason: [critical] Asarela was not a priest. He was a Levitical singer and musician. The Levite who served in the musical service did not have priestly duties. The role should be changed to 'singer' and 'musician'.; [major] According to 1 Chr 25:2, Asaph had sons named Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asarela (and possibly Shimei). The list of siblings potentially omits Shimei, but the four mentioned in verse 2 are correct. However, it should also be noted that 1 Chr 25:2 states Asaph had four sons, not three siblings plus Asarela. The sibling list should be verified.; [minor] The summary mentions 'temple service', but in David's time the temple had not yet been built—it was the tabernacle/tent sanctuary. The temple was first built by Solomon. The organization was a preparation for the temple, but the service took place in the tent. The text should be nuanced.; [minor] The title 'Levitical singer in the temple' is somewhat inaccurate, since the temple had not yet been built in David's time. It would be better to say 'Levitical singer and musician under David'.; [minor] The reference to 1 Chr 25:31 is incorrect in this context. Verse 31 concerns the twenty-fourth division (Romamti-Ezer), not Asarela's division. Asarela's/Jesarela's division is the seventh and is found in verse 14. The reference to verse 31 should be removed.; [minor] The event 'Service under Asaph's leadership' overlaps significantly with the first event and adds little new information. It could be considered merged.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Notes should be added regarding the name variation Asarela/Jesarela, and about the organization of temple service under David.

versions.summary: Asarelah (also called Jezarelah) was a son of Asaph, the famous worship leader during King David's time. He served as one of the Levitical singers and musicians, appointed by lot to lead worship. David organized 24 divisions of singers in preparation for the temple that Solomon would later build, and Asarelah was assigned to the seventh division. His service was part of the organized praise that David established for God's house, where music was regarded as a form of prophetic activity.

versions.reason: [minor] The second key event ('Service under Asaph's leadership') largely overlaps with the first event ('Appointment as singers and musicians'), since both refer to 1 Chr 25:2. Consider merging them or making the second more distinct.; [minor] The sentence 'Asarela was assigned to the seventh shift' is somewhat imprecise. It was the Jesarela form of the name that appears in 1 Chr 25:14, where the seventh lot fell. It may be helpful to clarify that the identification with the seventh shift is based on the name variation Jesarela.; [major] According to 1 Chr 25:2, Asaph had sons named Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asarela—but the brother Jesarela/Asarela variant is the same person. However, the list is incomplete: according to other passages in 1 Chr 25, more sons belong to the Asaph clan. Nevertheless, the main correction is that the list should match 1 Chr 25:2 exactly. As it stands, the sibling list is reasonable but possibly missing some names. The list is acceptable for 1 Chr 25:2.

footnotes.text: The name Asarelah (Hebrew: אֲשַׂרְאֵלָה) appears in 1 Chron 25:2, while the same person is called Jezarelah (יְשַׂרְאֵלָה) in 1 Chron 25:14. The name variations may be due to different transliterations or a scribal error in the Hebrew textual tradition. Both name forms contain the Hebrew element 'El' (God), and the prefix can mean 'God has made happy/right'.

The organization of the 24 divisions of singers under David (1 Chron 25) reflects a thorough structuring of worship in preparation for the coming temple. This system of casting lots ensured that the distribution was seen as divinely guided, not based on human favoritism.

Asaph, Asarelah's father, was one of the three chief worship leaders appointed by David (along with Heman and Jeduthun). The family of Asaph held a lasting place in Israelite worship tradition, and several psalms are attributed to Asaph (Ps 50, 73–83).

The use of the word 'prophesy' (Hebrew: נבא) in connection with the musical service (1 Chron 25:1–2) suggests that music in worship was understood as a form of prophetic activity—inspired communication of God's message through song and music. In rabbinic tradition, this was seen as confirmation that the inspiration of the Holy Spirit could come through musical worship.

Archaeological finds from the Iron Age in Israel/Judah, including depictions of musical instruments and inscriptions, confirm that organized music and singing held a central place in cultic practice in ancient Israel, consistent with the descriptions of temple service in Chronicles.
